rationale: A wins because it protects the founder from overclaiming: "Why Mindbody isn't charging extra for AI" turns a real bundled-pricing fact into a testable business story. B has energy, but "Mindbody Owns the Studio Software, the Consumer Marketplace, and Now the AI That Fills Both" leaps from ClassPass ownership to a platform story the update does not prove. Bigger is not better when the extra size comes from borrowed facts.
gaps_in_A: "Why Mindbody isn't charging extra for AI" is a real angle, but it still needs competitive pricing context before it becomes more than a sharp inference.
"small-business columnist at a regional business outlet" only works if a named local studio exists; otherwise that target gets mushy fast.
gaps_in_B: "Rolling Out to 50,000 Studios" overclaims the supplied fact. Mindbody powers booking for over 50,000 studios and salons; the update does not say the assistant is rolling out to all 50,000.
"While Fitness Apps Race to Build AI Coaches" imports a market narrative that was not in the update. Interesting frame, unsupported peg.
"the AI That Fills Both" implies a ClassPass/product integration the facts do not establish. The set asks the right question later, but the headline already committed the sin.
"Studio owner customer story — duplicate" is a bad kill. A named operator with real before-and-after economics would be one of the cleanest trade angles here.
